## Authors

Graeme Blair, University of California, Los Angeles

Simone Horowitz, University of California, Los Angeles

## Intro

We provide data on Customs and Border Protection on Title 8 encounters (including apprehensions and inadmissibles) and Title 42 expulsions. We provide three datasets: Apprehensions, Inadmissibles, and Encounters. 

Under Title 8, apprehension refers to those under physical control or temporary detainment by the United States Border Patrol (USBP) between Ports of Entry (POE) who are not lawfully in the United States, which may or may not result in an arrest. 

Under Title 8, inadmissible refers to those encountered at Ports of Entry (POE) who are determined to be inadmissible under immigration law by the Office of Field Operations (OFO). This can include those seeking lawful admission, asylum, or parole.

In this dataset, encounters refers specifically to USBP encounters, which include only Title 8 apprehensions and Title 42 expulsions and do not contain Title 8 inadmissibles recorded under the OFO. Generally, encounters refers to anyone apprehended by the United States Border Patrol (USBP) under Title 8 Apprehensions, encountered by the Office of Field Operations (OFO) under Title 8 Inadmissibles, or expelled under Title 42 Expulsions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an order under Title 42 that permitted expedited expulsions at and between ports of entry from March 2020 through May 11, 2023. After May 11, 2023, enforcement reverted to Title 8 Apprehensions and Inadmissibles. Title 42 Expulsions are tracked separately from immigration enforcement actions, including apprehension or inadmissibility, reported by CBP and are not based on immigration status.

We collected separate files published at different times on CBP’s website under Freedom of Information Act statistical records and present them in a single, usable dataset.

## Data Structure

Each row in the datasets represents one recorded CBP encounter involving an individual. Some records contain fields indicating that multiple individuals were encountered together. The datasets are maintained separately because they represent different enforcement categories, CBP components, source files, and record structures. Variant column names are merged under standardized headers that are used across all three datasets.

## Data Processing

It is important to note that files are identified by their URLs published on CBP’s website. If CBP replaces the contents of an existing URL the pipeline will not automatically detect this revision. We collected CBP data in these steps:

-   **Download apprehensions, inadmissibles, and encounters.** We identified and downloaded all relevant raw files from CBP’s original website. Any ambiguous files were manually reviewed.

-   **Profile header rows.** Here, we learned about the types of column names within each sheet to later build a crosswalk to match distinct column names to. The script separates sheets that fail profiling to be manually viewed only if they exist.

-   **Build a crosswalk of canonical column names.** We created a crosswalk from the distinct columns identified in the previous step to assign each a canonical column name and allow files within each dataset to be combined. This step was crucial to successfully condense variant columns that contain the same expected entries.

-   **Convert original files to cleaned format.** Then, we converted the headers in each dataset to their canonical name assigned in the crosswalk, ensuring that headers across sheets were standardized.

-   **Identify dataset overlaps.** We extracted the minimum and maximum encounter dates in each cleaned file, exploring whether duplicate datasets existed. Datasets with the same minimum and maximum date and equal row counts were flagged and manually examined.

-   **Remove duplicate datasets.** Upon examination, if files were determined to be exact duplicates, one copy was retained and the duplicate was excluded from stacking. If matching datasets contained complementary information, they were merged to retain the most complete version of each record.

-   **Stack unique datasets.** Unique datasets were stacked to yield our final apprehensions, inadmissibles, and encounters datasets.

-   **Build code maps.** We created lookup tables to translate coded values into readable values.

-   **Clean combined datasets.** Finally, combined datasets were cleaned to standardize redaction codes and whitespace, convert columns to appropriate data types, and order fields. Code maps were used to consolidate coded columns with their full-name column counterparts.

**Future work:** We are continuing to expand our datasets by submitting FOIA requests to obtain more recent datasets. We will update this codebook as processes develop.

## Warnings and Limitations

Below are some limitations and things to consider when accessing this data:

-   **Link permanence:** Files are identified by their URLs published on CBP’s website. If CBP replaces the contents of an existing URL the pipeline will not automatically detect this revision. 

-   **Redacted values:** At times, redacted codes were present in columns whose data types were cleaned. In this case, redacted codes were converted to NA values. If this occurred in a non-character column (i.e., columns that would convert redacted values to NAs), a companion flag column was created to indicate whether the NA was previously a redacted value. 

-   **Redaction codes:** CBP redaction codes used in released documents refer to standard Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) statutory exemptions. Common redaction codes that can be found in the data include:

    -   **Exemption (b)(7)(C):** To constitute an unwarranted invasion of the personal privacy of a third party/parties (in some instances by revealing an investigative interest in them).
    -   **Exemption (b)(7)(E):** Would disclose techniques and procedures for law enforcement investigations or prosecutions.

    More information can be found at [hhs.gov](https://www.hhs.gov/foia/exemptions-and-exclusions/index.html).

-   **Lack of subject identifiers:** Subject identification columns are some of the columns that CBP redacted. As such, identifying individual people rather than data entries was impossible to safely completely. When using or interpreting data, keep in mind that each row does not necessarily represent an individual.

-   **Missing values:** Missing values were not recorded in a standard fashion across datasets. Where some included "NA" values, others left cells blank. Many columns also contain redacted values. The differences in recording methods and missing information indications should be noted when interpreting this data.

-   **Excluded files:** As mentioned, if entire datasets were determined to be duplicates of each other, one was excluded from the final dataset. We have two instances of this, whose deletions we further explain here.

    -   **Apprehensions: `usbp_nationwide_apprehension_q4_fy_2024.xlsx`** was deleted and not merged. This file was concluded to be an erroneous duplicate of **`usbp_nationwide_apprehension_q3_fy_2024.xlsx`**, and thus, its data was discarded.

    -   **Inadmissibles: `ofo_inadmissible_case_by_case_feb_2025_0.xlsx`** was deleted and not merged. This file was found to be an exact duplicate of **`ofo_inadmissible_case_by_case_feb_2025.xlsx`** and contributed no new information.

-   **Overlapping dates:** Several raw Apprehension and Inadmissible datasets were found to record overlapping periods of time. In these instances, we retained broader datasets over more granular ones to prioritize consistency. `cbp/data/<dataset>/processed/<dataset>.stacked.parquet` contains both types.

-   **Column harmonization**: CBP lacks clear documentation about all of the headers included in our datasets. Our codebook indicates where intended meanings and methods of measurement were not apparent. Identical headers may not have had the same meaning across different datasets. Columns were merged to the best of our ability but still may contain errors.

-   **USBP vs. OFO Encounters**: Our Encounters dataset contains only encounters recorded by USBP, including Title 8 apprehensions and Title 42 expulsions. It excludes Title 8 inadmissibles recorded by OFO. Aggregated data on all encounters can be found on [CBP’s website](https://www.cbp.gov/document/stats/nationwide-encounters). Individual-level data is available only for USBP encounters.

-   **Manual function prompting:** Several scripts contain binary functions that must be manually set to `TRUE` or `FALSE` when updating data. Please visit the `README.md` for instructions on how to correctly run the scripts.
